items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: When players in the 60s came along — Coltrane, Miles Davis

ctx.x: aging, maturity, call it what you want. I choose my notes but it’s a matter of choice. I don’t think I — I listened to myself when I thought I was great, playing very intense stuff, and I haven’t liked it as much as I thought I did when I was playing it. You know what I mean? So I’m a firm believer in simplicity. Vic Dickinson was the master of that and I played next to him for eight of the ten years we were at Condon’s. Just a master of simplicity. And he had marvelous technique, but he would just lay it out…
When players in the 60s came along — Coltrane, Miles Davis — the music seemed to get, some of it, pretty angry. Was it something you listened to? Did it have an effect on you?

I just walked away from — I was not that interested. Some of the beautiful Miles Davis, you know the beautiful things, I loved it. The other agendas that go with the playing, the attitudes and things, I try not to let that get in the way of my playing. I think by that time I already had decided kind of where I was going to go musically and didn’t want to get into a lot of that, I thought it would mess my style. Of course I was working in the 60s, I was still working days, I hadn’t made my commitment to go full…
